doc.title: Jane Ira Bloom interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, March 3, 1998

title: Early piano, improvising and composing
summary: Piano from age four with Harvey Steinberg, improvising alongside written music, and supportive teachers.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: The other question I had was composing your own music is obviously very important to you. Did you have a time, can you remember the first time you wrote your own tune?

I was very young. I started studying piano, I think I was about four or five, four. And unlike other kind of classical early piano study, I began early on improvising and not knowing it. And I had a teacher who would show me what chord changes were and how to write things out, so that even when I was beginning to study the piano, I was also improvising at the same time. I didn’t know it. So my learning process went hand in hand, you know, improvising and studying written form as well. So it was not like it was anything exotic to me, it was just a part of what I did. And I think that’s why it seems so intuitive to me to do it.
It’s fortunate that you had a piano teacher that could give you a little support in that area.
Yeah. Harvey Steinberg. I’ll never forget him.
Thank you Harvey. You know because too often you hear the stories about people taking piano lessons and they want to try doing their own thing and it’s like, don’t do that.

Don’t do this don’t do that. No, music was pure joy for me. There was never anything associated with music other than pursuing a passion with a vengeance. I never had any bad experiences like that in my music education. I had terrific teachers and was very © Fillius Jazz Archive -6-
fortunate I think to live outside of Boston where I had access to a lot of great music training.
